title: Good Test Scores Can Hide a Bad Education
author: Vicky Brooks
summary: Vicky Brooks argues that treating higher test scores as proof of effective teaching confuses one measure of success with the purpose of education. She opens with a child who earns an A+ on a sustainability essay yet walks past litter on the playground. She traces the problem to the 1862 payment-by-results system and Donald Campbell's observation that a heavily weighted measure distorts what it measures. Using the performance versus learning distinction from Soderstrom and Bjork, she shows that a single test cannot tell the two apart. Her examples from reading, writing, migration and fair sharing show knowledge that never reaches how children act. She rejects the inquiry versus instruction framing and, citing Gert Biesta, asks educators to agree on what education is for before judging methods.
points: Brooks uses the history of payment by results to show that coaching for an exam can substitute for learning the skills it measures.
The performance versus learning distinction means a score on test day is an unreliable guide to what a child retains months later.
Concrete cases such as the reader who never reads again and the class that ignores a new pupil show knowledge failing to reach conduct.
She argues the debate is not inquiry versus instruction, since good inquiry includes explicit teaching and chances to use knowledge.
Citing Biesta, she says test scores capture only one of three purposes of education, so the question to ask of any method is better at what.
quotes: But raising test scores is not the same as improving education. We’ve confused one measure of success with the purpose of education itself.
In a narrow sense, it worked. Schools focused hard on what the inspectors would check. But one inspector, the poet Matthew Arnold, noticed what that focus cost.
A century later, the social scientist Donald Campbell described the same pattern: the more weight we place on a single measure, the more that measure bends the very thing it was meant to observe.

But what a child can do on the day of a test is an unreliable guide to what they’ll still understand months later. The psychologists Nicholas Soderstrom and Robert Bjork describe this as the difference between performance and learning.
A test can ask children to follow a recipe. Life asks them to cook.

Knowing how to divide the pizza is one thing. Knowing when equal isn’t fair requires something more than math. It requires judgment, and judgment grows when children use what they know in situations that matter to them.
Good inquiry doesn’t do that. Teachers explain and teach explicitly when children need it, and children also get chances to use that knowledge on their own.
Biesta puts the risk simply: we can end up valuing what we measure, instead of measuring what we value.
